questions.concept: Why Porifera are animals, not plants
questions.question: Sponges are sessile (fixed) like plants. Why are they classified as animals?
questions.solution: Classification follows body plan, not lifestyle: sponges lack cell walls and chlorophyll, feed by ingesting particles (heterotrophic), and their cells are totipotent with no true tissues. Fixed habit is an adaptation to filter-feeding, not plantness. Nutrition mode and cell structure decide the phylum.

questions.question: Why is the presence of a true coelom a major step in animal evolution?
questions.solution: A coelom (body cavity lined with mesoderm) suspends organs independently of the body wall — allowing them to grow, move and specialise; it also cushions them and enables a hydrostatic skeleton for burrowing. Flatworms (no coelom) are limited to flat, diffusion-dependent bodies. The coelom unlocked organ specialisation and larger body size.

questions.question: A snake and a mouse in the same forest handle temperature completely differently. Compare their strategies and energy costs.
questions.solution: Snake (ectotherm): body temperature follows the environment; it behaviourally basks/shades to regulate, spending almost no metabolic energy on heating — hence it can eat rarely. Mouse (endotherm): burns metabolic energy continuously to hold ~37 °C, staying active in cold but needing frequent food. Energy cost buys independence from the environment.

questions.concept: Insect success — why so many species
questions.question: Insects outnumber all other animal species combined. What adaptations account for this?
questions.solution: (1) Flight — dispersal and escape. (2) Exoskeleton — protection and water conservation, enabling terrestrial life. (3) Small size — many niches. (4) Metamorphosis — larvae and adults exploit different resources, avoiding self-competition. (5) Short generation time — fast adaptation. Niche partitioning plus mobility is the winning combination.

questions.question: Why does Nepal hold species from tiger to snow leopard within one small country?
questions.solution: Altitude spans ~60 m to 8,848 m, packing tropical, subtropical, temperate, alpine and nival zones side by side — each with its own climate, vegetation and fauna. Extreme topographic and climatic compression creates many habitats per unit area, hence high species richness. Elevation gradient = habitat diversity = biodiversity.

questions.question: Why do all members of a phylum share one basic body plan rather than each species inventing its own?
questions.solution: A body plan is fixed deep in development — a set of early embryonic decisions (symmetry, germ layers, segmentation, coelom) that later development elaborates on. Changing the plan means changing early developmental genes, which usually breaks the organism. Species diversify within the plan, not by replacing it. Deep homology constrains the possible forms.

questions.question: Over half of described animal species are arthropods. Give the structural and physiological reasons for this success.
questions.solution: (1) An exoskeleton gives protection, support and water conservation on land. (2) Segmented bodies with jointed appendages allow specialisation of limbs for walking, feeding, sensing and reproduction. (3) Small body size opens enormous numbers of micro-habitats. (4) Metamorphosis separates larval and adult niches. Arrangement plus protection plus small size proved exceptionally evolvable.

questions.question: An arthropod is vulnerable immediately after moulting. Why must it moult at all?
questions.solution: The rigid exoskeleton cannot grow or stretch, so the animal must shed it periodically to increase in size, then expand and harden a new one. Between shedding and hardening the body is soft and defenceless. Growth is therefore paid for with a recurring vulnerability window — a direct consequence of using hard external support.
